Project Overview

Goal: As analysts for a real estate agency, develop a model to predict the sale price of homes in Ames, Iowa.

Step 1: Data Cleaning and Preparation

Instructions from Professor:

  • Handle NA values by examining the meta-data and applying proper operations based on column nature
  • Identify columns where the vast majority of values are the same and consider removing them
  • Outlier Detection: Create a scatter plot of GrLivArea vs. SalePrice and identify outliers to remove

Data Import

train_data <- read.csv('train.csv', sep = ',', header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
test_data <- read.csv('test.csv', sep = ',', header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

Analysis: Successfully loaded training dataset with 1460 observations and 81 variables, and test dataset with 1459 observations.

Missing Values Analysis

cols_with_na <- colnames(train_data)[colSums(is.na(train_data)) > 0]
cat("Columns with missing values:\n")
## Columns with missing values:
print(cols_with_na)
##  [1] "LotFrontage"  "Alley"        "MasVnrType"   "MasVnrArea"   "BsmtQual"    
##  [6] "BsmtCond"     "BsmtExposure" "BsmtFinType1" "BsmtFinType2" "Electrical"  
## [11] "FireplaceQu"  "GarageType"   "GarageYrBlt"  "GarageFinish" "GarageQual"  
## [16] "GarageCond"   "PoolQC"       "Fence"        "MiscFeature"
cat("\nTotal columns with NA:", length(cols_with_na))
## 
## Total columns with NA: 19

Analysis: We identified 19 columns containing missing values. According to the dataset documentation, some NA values represent the absence of a feature (e.g., no pool, no garage) rather than missing data. We handled MasVnrArea by replacing NA with 0, as the absence of masonry veneer means 0 square feet.

train_data$MasVnrArea[is.na(train_data$MasVnrArea)] <- 0

Outlier Detection and Removal

ggplot(data = train_data, aes(x = GrLivArea, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Sale Price vs. Above Ground Living Area (Before Outlier Removal)",
       x = "Above Ground Living Area (sq ft)",
       y = "Sale Price ($)") +
  theme_minimal()

Analysis: The scatter plot reveals several extreme outliers - houses with very large living areas (>4,000 sq ft) but unexpectedly low sale prices. These anomalies could distort our predictive models and should be removed.

# Calculate mean and standard deviation for filtering
sale_mean <- mean(train_data$SalePrice, na.rm = TRUE)
sale_sd <- sd(train_data$SalePrice, na.rm = TRUE)
area_mean <- mean(train_data$GrLivArea, na.rm = TRUE)
area_sd <- sd(train_data$GrLivArea, na.rm = TRUE)

# Filter outliers (within 2 standard deviations)
train_data_filtered <- train_data %>%
  filter(SalePrice > (sale_mean - 2*sale_sd) &
         SalePrice < (sale_mean + 2*sale_sd) &
         GrLivArea > (area_mean - 2*area_sd) &
         GrLivArea < (area_mean + 2*area_sd))
ggplot(data = train_data_filtered, aes(x = GrLivArea, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "Sale Price vs. Above Ground Living Area (After Outlier Removal)",
       x = "Above Ground Living Area (sq ft)",
       y = "Sale Price ($)") +
  theme_minimal()

Analysis: After removing outliers using a 2-standard-deviation threshold, we reduced the dataset from 1460 to 1362 observations (6.7% reduction). The relationship between living area and sale price now shows a clearer positive correlation.

Step 2: Feature Transformation and Engineering

Instructions from Professor:

  • Logarithmic Transformation: Apply log transformation to SalePrice to normalize its skewed distribution
  • Creating Surface Area Features: Create a TotalSF feature for total house area
  • Encoding Ordinal Variables: Convert ordinal categorical features to numerical variables
  • Creating Temporal Features: Create a HouseAge variable

Logarithmic Transformation of Sale Price

# Display original SalePrice distribution
train_data_filtered_select <- train_data_filtered %>% select(SalePrice)
cat("Original SalePrice statistics:\n")
## Original SalePrice statistics:
cat("Mean:", mean(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
## Mean: 167938.9
cat("Median:", median(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
## Median: 157700
cat("Skewness: Right-skewed distribution\n\n")
## Skewness: Right-skewed distribution
# Apply log transformation
train_data_filtered <- train_data_filtered %>%
  filter(SalePrice > 0) %>%
  mutate(SalePrice = log10(SalePrice))

cat("Log-transformed SalePrice statistics:\n")
## Log-transformed SalePrice statistics:
cat("Mean:", mean(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
## Mean: 5.199855
cat("Median:", median(train_data_filtered$SalePrice), "\n")
## Median: 5.197831

Analysis: The logarithmic transformation successfully normalized the SalePrice distribution. This transformation is crucial because many regression algorithms assume normally distributed target variables, which improves model performance and prediction accuracy.

Creating Total Surface Area Feature

train_data_filtered <- train_data_filtered %>% 
  mutate(TotalSF = TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + X2ndFlrSF)

cat("TotalSF feature created successfully\n")
## TotalSF feature created successfully
cat("Range:", range(train_data_filtered$TotalSF), "\n")
## Range: 720 5048
cat("Mean:", mean(train_data_filtered$TotalSF), "sq ft\n")
## Mean: 2447.388 sq ft

Analysis: Created TotalSF by combining basement, first floor, and second floor areas.

Encoding Ordinal Variables

# Define quality mappings
qual_map <- c("None"=0, "Po"=1, "Fa"=2, "TA"=3, "Gd"=4, "Ex"=5)
bsmt_exposure_map <- c("None"=0, "No"=1, "Mn"=2, "Av"=3, "Gd"=4)
bsmtfin_map <- c("None"=0, "Unf"=1, "LwQ"=2, "Rec"=3, "BLQ"=4, "ALQ"=5, "GLQ"=6)
pool_map <- c("None"=0, "Fa"=1, "TA"=2, "Gd"=3, "Ex"=4)
fence_map <- c("None"=0, "MnWw"=1, "GdWo"=2, "MnPrv"=3, "GdPrv"=4)
functional_map <- c("Sal"=1, "Sev"=2, "Maj2"=3, "Maj1"=4, "Mod"=5, "Min2"=6, "Min1"=7, "Typ"=8)
landslope_map <- c("Sev"=1, "Mod"=2, "Gtl"=3)
paveddrive_map <- c("N"=0, "P"=1, "Y"=2)

# Apply mappings
train_data_filtered$ExterQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$ExterQual]
train_data_filtered$ExterCond_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$ExterCond]
train_data_filtered$BsmtQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtQual]
train_data_filtered$BsmtCond_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtCond]
train_data_filtered$HeatingQC_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$HeatingQC]
train_data_filtered$KitchenQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$KitchenQual]
train_data_filtered$FireplaceQu_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$FireplaceQu]
train_data_filtered$GarageQual_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$GarageQual]
train_data_filtered$GarageCond_num <- qual_map[train_data_filtered$GarageCond]
train_data_filtered$BsmtExposure_num <- bsmt_exposure_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtExposure]
train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType1_num <- bsmtfin_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType1]
train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType2_num <- bsmtfin_map[train_data_filtered$BsmtFinType2]
train_data_filtered$PoolQC_num <- pool_map[train_data_filtered$PoolQC]
train_data_filtered$Fence_num <- fence_map[train_data_filtered$Fence]
train_data_filtered$Functional_num <- functional_map[train_data_filtered$Functional]
train_data_filtered$LandSlope_num <- landslope_map[train_data_filtered$LandSlope]
train_data_filtered$PavedDrive_num <- paveddrive_map[train_data_filtered$PavedDrive]

cat("Ordinal variables successfully encoded to numerical format\n")
## Ordinal variables successfully encoded to numerical format
cat("Total ordinal features converted:", 17, "\n")
## Total ordinal features converted: 17

Analysis: Converted 17 ordinal categorical variables into numerical scales that preserve their inherent ordering. For example, quality ratings (Poor=1 to Excellent=5) now allow regression models to understand that “Excellent” is quantitatively better than “Good,” which is better than “Average.”

Feature Normalization

# Normalize numeric features (excluding target variables)
numeric_cols <- sapply(train_data_filtered, is.numeric)
numeric_names <- setdiff(names(train_data_filtered)[numeric_cols], 
                         c("SalePrice", "SalePrice_log"))
train_data_filtered[numeric_names] <- scale(train_data_filtered[numeric_names])

cat("Feature normalization completed\n")
## Feature normalization completed
cat("All numeric features now have mean ≈ 0 and standard deviation ≈ 1\n")
## All numeric features now have mean ≈ 0 and standard deviation ≈ 1

Analysis: Applied standardization (z-score normalization) to all numeric features. This ensures all variables are on the same scale (mean=0, sd=1), preventing features with larger magnitudes from dominating the model, particularly important for LASSO regression.

Step 3: Visualization and Exploration

Instructions from Professor:

  • Calculate correlation of all numerical variables with SalePrice and visualize top 15
  • Use box plots to show relationship between OverallQual and SalePrice
  • Create box plots comparing SalePrice across different Neighborhoods
  • Make scatter plot of SalePrice vs. TotalSF, colored by OverallQual
  • Add 2 additional pertinent visualizations

Impact of Overall Quality on Sale Price

ggplot(train_data_filtered, aes(x = factor(OverallQual), y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Impact of Overall Quality on Sale Price",
       x = "Overall Quality Rating",
       y = "Sale Price (Log Scale)") +
  theme_minimal()

Analysis: There is a strong positive relationship between Overall Quality and Sale Price. Houses rated 9-10 (Excellent) command significantly higher prices than those rated 1-5 (Poor to Average). The increasing median and range across quality levels demonstrates that quality is a major price driver.

Sale Price Distribution by Neighborhood

ggplot(train_data_filtered, aes(x = Neighborhood, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Sale Price Distribution by Neighborhood",
       x = "Neighborhood",
       y = "Sale Price (Log Scale)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Analysis: Neighborhood location substantially impacts home prices in Ames. Premium neighborhoods show consistently higher median prices and tighter distributions, while more affordable neighborhoods display lower medians with greater variability. Location is clearly a critical factor in property valuation.

Size-Price Relationship by Quality

ggplot(train_data_filtered, aes(x = TotalSF, y = SalePrice, color = as.factor(OverallQual))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Relationship Between Total Surface Area and Sale Price",
         x = "Total Surface Area (TotalSF, normalized)",
       y = "Sale Price (Log Scale)",
       color = "Overall Quality") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "RdYlGn")

Analysis: This visualization reveals a clear positive correlation between total surface area and sale price, with quality ratings adding an additional dimension. Higher quality homes (green/yellow) cluster in the upper right, showing that both size and quality independently contribute to higher prices.

Top 15 Features Correlated with Sale Price

numeric_vars <- sapply(train_data, is.numeric)
train_numeric <- train_data[, numeric_vars]
correlations <- cor(train_numeric, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_with_price <- correlations[, "SalePrice"]
top_corr <- sort(abs(cor_with_price), decreasing = TRUE)[1:15]

corr_df <- data.frame(
  Feature = names(top_corr),
  Correlation = top_corr
)

ggplot(corr_df, aes(x = reorder(Feature, Correlation), y = Correlation)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Features Most Correlated with Sale Price",
       x = "Features",
       y = "Correlation (Absolute Value)") +
  theme_minimal()

Analysis: The correlation analysis identifies OverallQual, GrLivArea, GarageCars, GarageArea, and TotalBsmtSF as the top predictors. These features will be prioritized in our predictive models. Interestingly, both quality metrics and size-related features dominate, confirming our earlier observations.

Additional Visualization 1: Construction Year Impact

ggplot(train_data_filtered, aes(x = YearBuilt, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Impact of Construction Year on Sale Price",
       x = "Year Built",
       y = "Sale Price (Log Scale)") +
  theme_minimal()

Analysis: A clear upward trend shows that newer homes typically sell for higher prices. The red LOESS curve reveals this relationship is approximately linear, with some acceleration for very recent constructions. Home age is evidently an important pricing factor. Note that Year Built datas are normalized.

Additional Visualization 2: Number of Rooms vs. Sale Price

ggplot(train_data_filtered, aes(x = TotRmsAbvGrd, y = SalePrice, 
                                 color = as.factor(OverallQual))) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.6, width = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "Number of Rooms Above Ground vs. Sale Price",
       subtitle = "Colored by Overall Quality rating",
       x = "Total Rooms Above Ground",
       y = "Sale Price (Log Scale)",
       color = "Overall Quality") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "RdYlGn")

Analysis: More rooms generally correlate with higher prices, but this relationship is moderated by quality. High-quality homes (green) with more rooms achieve premium prices, while lower-quality homes (red) show a weaker room-count effect. This suggests room quantity and quality interact in determining value.

Step 4: Modeling and Prediction

Instructions from Professor:

  • Train a Multiple Linear Regression model as baseline using best features
  • Train a LASSO regression model for automatic feature selection
  • Train a Random Forest model
  • Evaluate model performance using multiple indicators and interpret important features

Feature Selection for Modeling

features <- c("SalePrice", "OverallQual", "GrLivArea", "GarageCars", "GarageArea",
              "TotalBsmtSF", "X1stFlrSF", "FullBath", "TotRmsAbvGrd",
              "YearBuilt", "YearRemodAdd", "GarageYrBlt")

data_selected <- train_data_filtered %>% select(all_of(features))
data_selected <- na.omit(data_selected)
data_selected$LogSalePrice <- log(data_selected$SalePrice)

cat("Selected", length(features)-1, "features for modeling\n")
## Selected 11 features for modeling
cat("Final dataset size:", nrow(data_selected), "observations\n")
## Final dataset size: 1284 observations

Analysis: Based on correlation analysis, we selected 11 features representing quality metrics, size measurements, and temporal characteristics. These features capture the key drivers of home prices identified in our exploratory analysis.

Model 1: Multiple Linear Regression

model_lm <- lm(LogSalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + GarageCars + GarageArea +
                 TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + FullBath + TotRmsAbvGrd +
                 YearBuilt + YearRemodAdd + GarageYrBlt,

Model 2: LASSO Regression

Y <- log(data_selected$SalePrice)
X <- as.matrix(data_selected %>% select(-SalePrice, -LogSalePrice))

lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X, Y, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
best_lambda <- lasso_cv$lambda.min

cat("Optimal lambda value:", best_lambda, "\n\n")
## Optimal lambda value: 3.133926e-05
lasso_model <- glmnet(X, Y, alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda)
print(lasso_model)
## 
## Call:  glmnet(x = X, y = Y, alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda) 
## 
##   Df  %Dev    Lambda
## 1 11 80.26 3.134e-05

Analysis: LASSO regression with cross-validation identified the optimal regularization parameter (lambda = 3.1^{-5}). LASSO’s automatic feature selection shrinks less important coefficients toward zero, potentially improving generalization by reducing overfitting compared to standard linear regression.

Model 3: Random Forest

rf_model <- randomForest(
  LogSalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea + GarageCars + GarageArea +
    TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + FullBath + TotRmsAbvGrd +
    YearBuilt + YearRemodAdd + GarageYrBlt,
  data = data_selected,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 4,
  importance = TRUE,
  na.action = na.omit
)

print(rf_model)
##

##  randomForest(formula = LogSalePrice ~ OverallQual + GrLivArea +      GarageCars + GarageArea + TotalBsmtSF + X1stFlrSF + FullBath +      TotRmsAbvGrd + YearBuilt + YearRemodAdd + GarageYrBlt, data = data_selected,      ntree = 500, mtry = 4, importance = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)

## No. of variables tried at each split: 4

Analysis: The Random Forest model with 500 trees explains 80% of variance (pseudo R²). This ensemble method captures non-linear relationships and interactions between features that linear models might miss. The mean of squared residuals indicates good predictive accuracy.

Model Evaluation and Comparison

# Charger le jeu de test filtré
features <- c("SalePrice", "OverallQual", "GrLivArea", "GarageCars", "GarageArea",
              "TotalBsmtSF", "X1stFlrSF", "FullBath", "TotRmsAbvGrd",
              "YearBuilt", "YearRemodAdd", "GarageYrBlt")

data_selected <- train_data_filtered %>% select(all_of(features))
data_selected <- na.omit(data_selected)

# Conversion de SalePrice en numérique
data_selected$SalePrice <- as.numeric(data_selected$SalePrice)

actual_prices <- log(data_selected$SalePrice)

# Jeu de test pour la prédiction
test_data <- data_selected %>% select(-SalePrice)

# Fonction d’évaluation
evaluate_model <- function(actual, predicted) {
  data.frame(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((predicted - actual)^2)),
    MAE  = mean(abs(predicted - actual)),
    R2   = cor(actual, predicted)^2,
    MAPE = mean(abs((predicted - actual) / actual)) * 100
  )
}

# --- Modèle linéaire ---
pred_lm <- exp(predict(model_lm, newdata = test_data)) 
results_lm <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lm)

# --- Modèle LASSO ---
pred_lasso <- exp(predict(lasso_model, s = best_lambda, newx = as.matrix(test_data)))  
results_lasso <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lasso)

# --- Modèle Random Forest ---
pred_rf <- exp(predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data)) 
results_rf <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_rf)

# --- Comparaison ---

results_lm <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lm)
results_lasso <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_lasso)
results_rf <- evaluate_model(exp(actual_prices), pred_rf)

colnames(results_lasso) <- c("RMSE", "MAE", "R2", "MAPE")


# Combiner dans un data.frame propre
results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Linear_Regression", "LASSO", "Random_Forest"),
  RMSE  = c(results_lm$RMSE, results_lasso$RMSE, results_rf$RMSE),
  MAE   = c(results_lm$MAE, results_lasso$MAE, results_rf$MAE),
  R2    = c(results_lm$R2, results_lasso$R2, results_rf$R2),
  MAPE  = c(results_lm$MAPE, results_lasso$MAPE, results_rf$MAPE)
)

print(results)
##               Model       RMSE        MAE        R2      MAPE
## 1 Linear_Regression 0.06228360 0.04443707 0.8069216 0.8587365
## 2             LASSO 0.06229326 0.04440487 0.8068561 0.8580827
## 3     Random_Forest 0.02845567 0.01944324 0.9635088 0.3754695

Overall Model Performance:

  • Random Forest achieves the best performance with the lowest RMSE (0.03) and highest R² (0.9635), capturing complex non-linear relationships
  • LASSO shows competitive performance with RMSE of 0.06, benefiting from feature selection
  • Linear Regression provides a solid baseline with RMSE of 0.06

The Random Forest model is recommended for deployment due to its superior predictive accuracy.

Comparison Visualizations

# RMSE Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = RMSE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(RMSE, 2)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Lower is better - measures average prediction error",
       y = "RMSE ($)", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

RMSE Analysis: Random Forest shows the lowest RMSE, meaning its predictions deviate least from actual prices on average. This represents approximately 0.4% error relative to home values.

# R² Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = R2, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 3)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "R² (Coefficient of Determination) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Higher is better - proportion of variance explained",
       y = "R²", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

R² Analysis: Random Forest explains 96.4% of price variance, demonstrating excellent predictive power. All models exceed 80% explained variance, indicating strong overall performance.

# MAE Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = MAE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(MAE, 2)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Mean Absolute Error (MAE) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Lower is better - average absolute prediction error",
       y = "MAE ($)", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

MAE Analysis: MAE provides an interpretable metric - Random Forest predictions are off by approximately $0 on average, making it highly reliable for real-world pricing decisions.

# MAPE Comparison
ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = MAPE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(MAPE, 2), "%")), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) Comparison",
       subtitle = "Lower is better - average percentage prediction error",
       y = "MAPE (%)", x = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

MAPE Analysis: With a MAPE of 0.38%, Random Forest provides predictions within 0% of actual sale prices on average - an excellent result for real estate valuation.

Conclusions and Recommendations

With our work, we started with data and after research to determine each data point, we needed to clean, transform, and after that, test with different linear models to predict the price of houses. We learned during this project that it is important to have clean data and it’s especially important to use the good data for linear models to predict results, in our case, the price of houses in Ames, Iowa. And when we compared different models and evaluated them, we used different accuracy metrics to select which one is better in our case. For us, and for our project, it’s Random Forest; it has better performance than the others. So, as we are analysts for a real estate agency, with our tool, in this case, our model that we have developed, our agency can use it to determine the price of a house by entering different information about the house features: “SalePrice”, “OverallQual”, “GrLivArea”, “GarageCars”, “GarageArea”, “TotalBsmtSF”, “X1stFlrSF”, “FullBath”, “TotRmsAbvGrd”, “YearBuilt”, “YearRemodAdd”, “GarageYrBlt”. We have determined that these features are the best to determine a probable price of a house. In the future, we can develop an app or website to help real estate agents.
